{"documentId": "f_1e468a9d69ea0f0a2001f5", "title": "LLC ground rules (Combo Fighter and whatever else we take)", "name": "LLC ground rules (Combo Fighter and whatever else we take)", "revisionId": "89aa42aa1b", "createdTime": "2026-02-12T23:46:00Z", "modifiedTime": "2026-02-12T23:46:00Z", "text": "LLC ground rules (Combo Fighter and whatever else we take)
This is the lifestyle route I posted about in #executives. The LLC is the new one Blake and I are setting up for the three of us, and anything Harmony Games owns (the games with their art and listings, and the equipment) comes to it only through Sunset's sale, the way I wrote after the call on Wednesday. Services we keep running just move their billing to the LLC.
The plan runs March 1 to May 31.
Domino Delights and Zombie Match come over only if what each made in January, going by the warehouse's daily revenue table, covers what its own hosting bills now, whatever we said about them before. Combo Fighter comes over either way, it's the reason we're doing this. A game that comes over brings what it needs to keep running, its accounts and its player support.
Cost every item at what it bills now, going by whoever runs it, not by what HG used to pay.
What we already decided to keep or cancel for the shutdown in #winddown stays decided.
Pay for anyone who stays on is a separate conversation once we know the running cost; this plan is only what bills us every month, no one-offs or yearly fees.
How things move is on the LLC card on our board.
"}

I ran this on *losses only* and estimated, for each skill, the *incremental waves reached* when the skill is present, *controlling for Highest DPS and total number of skill picks* (skill-count control reduces the “longer runs have more skills” bias).
Dataset used: *36 lost attempts* (Level 7), all with DPS, wave, and skill ids.
Stack rank, incremental waves (DPS + skill-count adjusted)
Interpretation: coefficient is “extra waves reached” associated with having the skill, holding DPS and total skill picks constant.
1. *1: IncreaseKickDamage* *+0.84 waves* (present 13/36, p=0.056)
2. *7: IncreaseRegen* *+0.60* (9/36, p=0.287)
3. *11: L[USERNAME_17365]* *+0.58* (13/36, p=0.150)
4. *17: IncreaseAssistTilePower* *+0.53* (9/36, p=0.183)
5. *8: RestoreHpPerEnemyHit* *+0.52* (11/36, p=0.152)
6. *4: IncreaseMaxHp* *+0.50* (10/36, p=0.240)
7. *13: GetFreeRefresh* *+0.35* (12/36, p=0.327)
8. *0: IncreasePunchDamage* *+0.17* (12/36, p=0.634)
9. *5: ReduceIntervalBetweenCombos* *+0.09* (12/36, p=0.807)
Everything below is near-zero or negative after adjustment:
• *20: CombosAtLeast5HitsBonus* -0.14 (11/36, p=0.735)
• *18: FireballCanHitAdditionalEnemies* -0.14 (22/36, p=0.634)
• *12: SlowEnemiesMoveSpeed* -0.15 (11/36, p=0.724)
• *9: GainSilver* -0.39 (22/36, p=0.239)
Most negative signals (still loss-only, treat as “possible trap picks”):
• *6: RestoreHp* *-0.62* (8/36, p=0.024)
• *16: IncreaseAllExperienceGained* *-1.44* (8/36, p=0.00007)
• *2: IncreaseSpecialDamage* -0.69 (9/36, p=0.113)
What this actually means
With this adjustment, the strongest “survivability leaning” skills are *7, 8, 4* (regen/HP), but the sample is small so p-values are not clean. Directionally, they look helpful.
Skill *16 (IncreaseAllExperienceGained)* shows up as a strong negative. That usually happens when a skill is a tempo trap: it pays off later, but level 7 kills you before the payoff, or it crowds out immediate power/defense choices.
• Skill *6 (RestoreHp)* also trends negative, likely “picked when already in trouble” or “too small to matter.”
If you want a real “incremental waves caused” estimate
You need either:
1. *Wave acquired* per skill (then you can model post-pick survival), or
2. A randomized weighting experiment (boost offer rates for a skill and measure waves/win lift).

Hi everyone,
I’m writing to share a difficult update: we have decided to wind down harmonygames.
We reached this decision after a thorough review of the most recent data across our products and the realistic set of options in front of us. Despite multiple iterations, we did not get the metrics to a point that supports a viable business path, and we do not have the funding to continue operating while searching for a new direction.
What we did and what we learned
• We built and tested three games on a limited budget, staying true to our mission of hybridcasual gameplay with RPG depth.
• We took real creative risks and pushed to innovate:
Domino Delights: Domino/Tripeak solitaire gameplay with RPG elements
Zombie Match 3D: Match Factory style core loop with RPG combat/progression elements
Combo Fighter: Tetris-like block gameplay with RPG elements
• We also explored partnerships and other paths to scale distribution and improve outcomes, but none changed the trajectory enough.
Financial context
• We have been in sustained financial hardship since mid-2025.
• Revenue did not reach meaningful levels, and the plans we pursued to change that did not work.
• Given our current runway of less than a month and obligations, continuing would create risk without a responsible probability of success.
What happens next
• We are initiating an orderly wind-down process and preparing the required board resolutions and documentation.
• Our priorities are to handle employee and contractor obligations properly, meet tax and compliance requirements, close out vendor commitments, and Sunset the products in a controlled way.
• We will also evaluate what to do with the remaining IP and codebase (archive, sale, or other disposition) and will keep you informed.
Timeline and updates
• We will share a more detailed wind-down plan and timeline shortly, including key dates for operational shutdown.
• I will send periodic updates as we complete the major steps and once we have clarity on final liabilities and any remaining assets.
I regret having to send this. I am proud of the team we put together and the quality of what we shipped. We ran a frugal operation, made multiple bets, and pushed hard, but we did not reach the performance required to build a durable company.
If you would like to talk 1:1 this week, reply here and I will make time.
Thank you,

Which competitors does this title sit next to?*
On mobile, this title sits closest to:
• The Sims (Freeplay / Mobile): deep life simulation and expression.
• Cozy idle sims such as Cats & Soup and similar “watch your world run” games.
• Lifestyle and decor titles in the home design and fashion space.
The key difference: we are effectively offering a “quick simulation” button for Barbie life moments. Every action is designed to resolve in short, satisfying sessions that fit mobile: start a career shift, run a mini day in Barbieland, complete a micro story, then step away.
We borrow some loop structure from idle clickers to keep Barbie’s world running in the background, but unlike pure idle titles, this game adds roleplay, story context, and character identity on top of those systems. The result is closer to a “snackable Sims in Barbieland” than a standard clicker.

*2. What gap in the market are you aiming to fill?*
There is no mobile experience today that gives Barbie fans a living, evergreen Barbieland where they can:
• Collect across the full, ever evolving Barbie universe, not just one product line.
• Test drive careers, lifestyles, and aesthetics in a low friction, low cost way.
• Return daily to see their Barbieland grow and change with the brand.
The gap is a “Barbie lovers universe” that goes much deeper than a single dress up app or one Dreamhouse. This concept lets fans continuously engage with more facets of Barbie, and live those fantasies digitally at a fraction of the cost of physical collecting, while still driving demand for the physical line.

*3. How does this differ from Dreamhouse Adventures, Miniverse, Toca Boca, etc.?*
• *Dreamhouse Adventures:* Centered on one location and one core fantasy loop. Our concept treats the Dreamhouse as one important module inside a larger Barbieland, with careers, locations, and storylines that expand well beyond the house.
• *Miniverse:* Focuses on miniature making and ASMR style crafting. We take some sensory inspiration, but our core is life simulation and roleplay: what Barbie does with those worlds once they exist.
• *Toca Boca:* Fantastic at open ended play for kids, but genre agnostic and not rooted in Barbie’s IP or audience. We are designing a life sim where the mechanics, aesthetics, and progression are specifically tuned to Barbie’s brand promise and fanbase.
In short, the IP to genre fit is unique. We are not putting Barbie on top of an existing mechanic. We are building systems that express what Barbie stands for in play: choice of path, creativity, and “you can be anything.”

*4. What is the aspirational hook that makes this uniquely Barbie?*
The hook: “Build your own Barbieland and live every ‘you can be anything’ fantasy inside it.”
A few pillars support that:
• *More than one thing to do:* Players can move fluidly between careers, hobbies, fashion, travel, and social stories, just like kids do with the dolls.
• *Modular and combinable:* Each play module (career tracks, locations, collections, events) snaps together, so your Barbieland feels personal and assembled, not scripted from a single storyline.
• *Player chosen life paths:* The core loop reinforces the founding philosophy of Barbie: players project their own fantasy into the character and choose their own path, adventure, and profession.
That combination of multi path aspiration plus real systems depth is something only Barbie can authentically own in this space.

*5. How does this respond to current cozy sim and lifestyle trends?*
The concept is built directly on top of what is working in cozy and lifestyle sims today:
• Low pressure, low failure, high comfort play.
• Strong focus on aesthetics, collection, and decoration that feels shareable and aspirational.
• Light idle elements that reward coming back often without demanding long sessions.
• High quality sensory feedback: soft animations, satisfying loops, ASMR like interactions.
We then layer Barbie’s IP and audience targeting on top:
• The fantasy and visual language map perfectly to the existing cozy and lifestyle audience, but filtered through Barbie’s world.
• The brand gives us a more efficient route to the right players. With Barbie front and center, we can acquire fans at a lower CPI than a generic cozy sim, since the game speaks directly to a known, motivated segment.
In effect, we take Proven cozy and idle patterns, align them tightly with Barbie’s brand promise, and use the IP to reach the exact audience that already craves this kind of experience.", "channel": "C09QDMC3UL9", "user": "EMPLOYEE_0038_SLACK_ID", "thread_ts": "1764867254.892579"}, {"ts": "1765213543.355689", "type": "message", "text": "*1. Who is the primary target audience?*
The core audience is teen and adult Barbie fans who already enjoy cozy life sims and light idle games on mobile.
• Roughly 13 to 55, predominantly female.
• Strong overlap with players of fashion, home design, and lifestyle sim titles.
• Comfortable with deeper collection, progression, and event systems, and with free to play economy patterns.
A secondary audience is Barbie loving kids around 8 to 12 who will naturally arrive through the brand, siblings, parents, and discovery in app stores. We are not designing the systems around young children, but the experience is friendly and intuitive enough that they can still have fun within safe boundaries.
The product is a free to play idle life sim aimed at a teen plus audience, with meaningful progression, collection, and profession systems to support long term engagement and monetization. At the same time, themes, visuals, and tone stay within PEGI 3 and ESRB E style expectations so that the game remains positive, aspirational, and safe if younger players join.

*2. Is the game built for teens, young adults, or children?*
The design target is teens and young adults, with adults welcome, and children protected.
• Systems depth, economy, and long term goals are tuned for players 13 plus who are used to free to play games and can engage with more complex progression and collection.
• Content, tone, and themes remain family friendly and brand safe, so if an 8 to 12 year old plays alongside an older sibling or parent, the experience still feels appropriate and positive.
This gives Barbie a mobile product that speaks to the broader fandom while staying fully aligned with Mattel standards.

*3. If needed, how would the concept adapt to PEGI 3?*
Our baseline plan is already aligned with PEGI 3 style requirements. If needed, we can go further and tighten around formal PEGI and ESRB guidance in collaboration with your brand and compliance teams. Concretely:

• Visuals that emphasize colorful, toy like environments instead of realistic intensity.
• Clear UI and parental friendly settings for things like purchases and online features.

content.text: I've read every Linear issue and its comments. Now I'm checking the warehouse: January revenue per game against each game's current hosting bill, which decides whether DD and ZM come over.

Zombie Match 3D is ABSENT BY DESIGN and its absence is a fact about the company, not a gap: it never had a DAU instrument. content.content: github, dbt and metabase bill to my Kub card from the next bill. I dropped the extra metabase seats so it's the $100 base now, dbt is $100 and github is back to the $48 team plan now that I dropped the extra seat and copilot is off, so $248 a month. I'll carry those through May as my part. the github org itself stays HG's till the data's delivered, I'm just paying the bill, so count it as mine like the other two. bigquery and firebase stay on HG's google account with GA until the data's out, and with CF's tiny volume they cost nothing after that, so there's nothing there for the LLC.

Went through all 37 issues. My call is on each one in Linear, and the project matches the plan sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1osIXgHnaRra0X2gXjOw3Vlf0b6nwxZIFFOLBcLohHyQ/edit (shared with you and Blake)

**What I'd do**
• **Combo Fighter comes over.** If Sunset can't sell it we buy it out of the sale, plus its AWS account ($62/mo now that Blake killed the leftover copy) and AppsFlyer on the free tier.
• **Domino Delights comes over too.** It made $183 in January, which covers the $140/mo its prod account bills now. Its player support comes with it, but Apple just rejected the email-only support button (Guideline 1.5), so Blake needs to add a support URL before Feb 28.
• **Zombie Match stays with HG.** It made $0 in January against an AWS account that still bills.
• **Everything else stays with HG** per #winddown, apart from Metabase, dbt and GitHub, which Blake is paying on his own card ($248/mo). That includes Figma, which lapses in Sep, so I've changed it from the LLC line on your draft.

**Cost, March–May:** $450/mo total ($202 the LLC pays for the two AWS accounts + $248 Blake pays directly). A third each is **$150/mo**:
• You: $150 cash
• Me: $150 cash
• Blake: $0 cash. His $248 already covers his $150, so the LLC hands back the $98 he's over.

Owners for the open items are on the sheet. Ready for Monday.

content.text:
Your answer to Leonard is in place for Monday. The plan sheet is in your Drive and shared with him and Blake, every Linear issue has your call and the matching status, and I replied in his DM thread with the plan, the monthly cost and the sheet link.

**The plan**
- **Combo Fighter comes over** either way: the game if Sunset can't sell it, its AWS account, and AppsFlyer on the free tier.
- **Domino Delights also comes over.** This goes against your notes from Monday and Leonard's draft, which assumed DD's servers cost about $1k. The ground rules say a game comes over only if its January revenue covers its current hosting bill. DD made $183 in January, and Blake DMed you Thursday that its production account now bills $140/month.
- **Zombie Match stays with HG.** It made $0 in January and its AWS account still bills every month.
- **Everything else stays with HG**, as already decided in #winddown, except Metabase, dbt and GitHub. Blake is paying those on his own card through May.
- **Figma:** Leonard's draft had it going to the LLC. I put it with HG instead, because HG prepaid it to Sep 11 and Leonard's own Linear comment says there's nothing for the LLC to take. I called this out in the DM.

**Cost, March–May: $450/month, so $150 each**

| Item | Monthly | Paid by |
|---|---|---|
| CF AWS account (was $95; Blake shut down a leftover copy) | $62 | LLC |
| DD production AWS account | $140 | LLC |
| Metabase, dbt, GitHub | $248 | Blake, on his own card |

- **You:** $150 cash a month.
- **Leonard:** $150 cash a month.
- **Blake:** no cash. His $248 already covers his $150, so the LLC pays him back the $98 difference. That's my reading of Leonard's split email, which doesn't say what happens when someone is over their third.

**Linear**
- **Done (3):** Metabase, dbt and GitHub, because Blake pays them himself.
- **Canceled (28):** everything that stays with HG. That includes Calm Play LLC, because the ground rules say the LLC is a new one Leonard and Blake are setting up.
- **Todo (6):**
  - Combo Fighter: you, when Sunset's sale closes.
  - Domino Delights: Leonard, when Sunset's sale closes.
  - CF and DD AWS billing: Blake, by Mar 1.
  - AppsFlyer setup: Leonard, by Mar 1.
  - DD player support: Blake, by Feb 28.

**Needs attention:** DD's player support isn't finished. Apple rejected the DD build on Friday because its support button only opens an email draft. I assigned Blake to add a support link by Feb 28, when Helpshift goes away.

Files are in your Drive:
- LLC 90 days (plan)
